newsitem.title: USA: CBOT defends corn/soybean delivery change proposal.
newsitem.headline: CBOT defends corn/soybean delivery change proposal.

text.p: The Chicago Board of Trade on Thursday defended its proposed delivery changes in the corn and soybean futures contracts and said there were no "legal or economic reasons" for the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to reject it.
At a public hearing held by the CFTC, the CBOT described its proposed changes as "balanced and thoughtful" and designed to meet all requirements set forth by the agency.

"No delivery system can be perfect," said Bill Evans, chairman of the CBOT's grain delivery task force, in written testimony prepared for the hearing. "The design of a delivery system necessarily involves trade-offs."

Under pressure by the CFTC to change the delivery terms to reflect dwindling storage capacity in Chicago, the CBOT proposed to eliminate the ports of Toledo and St. Louis as delivery points. The exchange would like to replace them with a single delivery area with 34 shipping points along the northern Illinois River.
But politicians from Ohio and farm groups throughout the midwest have objected to the plan, claiming it would make the futures market more susceptible to price manipulation.

"The CBOT proposal is the only balanced and thoughtful proposal on the table, it meets all the requirements set forth by the CFTC, and there are no legal or economic reasons for the CFTC to reject it," Evans said.

The agency last month urged the CBOT to reconsider its proposal, and reinstate the port of Toledo. If the CFTC does not approve the proposal, the agency has the power to publish its own proposed changes in the delivery points of the contracts, an action likely to prompt a legal challenge by the exchange, according to experts.

"No delivery system could be constructed that would eliminate the chance of manipulation by either the long or the short (positions)," Evans said. "However, by tying the delivery system to the flow of one of the world's most active cash markets in terms of production and use, the CBOT's proposal comfortably meets the Commodity Exchange Act's requirement that delivery terms tend to prevent or diminish manipulation."

Ohio Rep. Marcy Kaptur (D-Ohio) as well as representatives of Cargill Inc, Archer Daniels Midland, the Michigan state agriculture commission, the American Soybean Association and other groups were also scheduled to testify at the public hearing.
